title: Non-reciprocity drives a Brownian dimer out of equilibrium
authors: Suman Pramanik, Soham Dutta, Arnab Saha
abstract: We consider the minimal model of a two dimensional Brownian dimer consisting of two overdamped monomers, trapped in an isotropic harmonic potential and mutually coupled by a non-reciprocal harmonic spring that violates Newton's action-reaction principle. We have shown that the non-reciprocal interaction alone can drive the system far from equilibrium, in the absence of any external time dependent drive and being in contact with a single thermal bath. The exact steady state probability distribution and current are explicitly calculated for the zero-rest-length limit of the spring, which eventually maps our model to another non-equilibrium phenomenon, called Brownian gyration. For a spring with finite rest length, these quantities are calculated numerically.
summary: The authors investigate the steady-state dynamics of a Brownian dimer coupled by a non-reciprocal spring. They prove that breaking Newton's action-reaction principle alone is sufficient to generate a persistent current, driving the system far from equilibrium without external temperature gradients. The methodology involves advanced statistical mechanics techniques applied to Langevin dynamics.
main_problem: To determine if a system can reach a non-equilibrium steady state, characterized by a persistent current or directed motion, solely due to internal non-reciprocal interactions without external driving forces like temperature gradients.
main_result: Non-reciprocity in the coupling spring is sufficient to generate a non-zero stationary current ($\mathbf{J} \propto (k_2 - k_1)$), demonstrating that breaking Newton's action-reaction principle can drive a system out of equilibrium even at constant temperature.
method: The analysis uses overdamped Langevin equations and the Fokker-Planck formalism to calculate the steady-state probability distribution, current ($\mathbf{J}$), and vorticity (curl of $\mathbf{J}$).
model_or_system: A two-dimensional Brownian dimer consisting of two overdamped monomers trapped in an isotropic harmonic potential and coupled by a non-reciprocal harmonic spring. The analysis covers the analytically solvable zero-rest-length limit ($l=0$) and extends to finite rest lengths.
key_observables: Steady-state current ($\mathbf{J}$), local vorticity (curl of $\mathbf{J}$), and the stationary joint probability distribution $P(x_1, x_2)$.
important_parameters:
Non-reciprocity strength ($k_1 
eq k_2$), temperature difference/bath coupling ($T_1$ vs $T_2$), and spring rest length ($l$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the linear dynamics derived from the Langevin equations for the $l=0$ case, and uses matrix methods (Lyapunov equation) to find stationary solutions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate joint probability distributions showing non-factorizable correlations due to non-reciprocity, and visualize the vorticity structure, which exhibits a central vortex core surrounded by an anti-vortex ring when currents are present.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the current generation mechanism by first establishing the general framework using the Fokker-Planck equation for linear systems ($l=0$). It then shows that non-reciprocity alone generates current, and finally generalizes this to include temperature gradients, demonstrating the interchangeability of these two symmetry-breaking mechanisms.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean theoretical demonstration of how microscopic violations of fundamental symmetries (like action-reaction) can lead to macroscopic, persistent non-equilibrium phenomena in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant for understanding energy dissipation and transport in complex materials.

Heatmap of the joint probability distribution of two variates, obtained by numerically integrating the Langevin equations (for l = 0): Top — P(x1, x2) [identical for {y1, y2}], Bottom — P(x1, y1) [identical for {x1, y2}, etc.]. Note the distinctly different spread and alignment of the two distribution profiles. This is simply because:P(x1, y1) = R dx2dy2P(x1, x2, y1, y2) = R dx2dy2P(x1, x2)P(y1, y2) = R dx2P(x1, x2) R dy2P(y1, y2) = P(x1)P(y1), and so on. However, this is not true for P(x1, x2) or P(y1, y2). The color scale indicates the value of probability. The values of the pa- rameters used in simulation are: k0 = 1, T = 1, γ = 1, k1 = 1, k2 = 5.

FIG. 3. Heatmap of the magnitude of current of two variates with an overlay of the stream plot of the current vector, ob- tained by numerically integrating the Langevin equations (for l = 0): Top — in the {x1, x2} plane [identical for {y1, y2}], Bottom — in the {x1, y1} plane [identical for {x1, y2}, etc.]. Note the absence of vorticity in the latter case. This implies the average current is non-zero in x1 −x2 (or, y1 −y2) plane but zero in x1 −y1 (or, x2, y2) plane.
